content: During periods of peak activity in high-risk areas, targeted outreach programs are implemented to promote the use of harm reduction services. These initiatives distribute condoms, provide prevention information, and offer referrals to appropriate services. Public health centers and hospitals collaborate closely with these efforts, delivering both therapeutic and preventive services, such as methadone maintenance therapy (MMT) and needle and syringe programs (NSP), alongside safe injecting advice. Strong partnerships with law enforcement, the National Narcotics Board, the Ministry of Social Affairs, and the justice system enhance engagement with key stakeholders and duty bearers. Program activities are meticulously tracked through monthly data submissions from all partners, and annual surveys assess participant behaviors and satisfaction with services, including HIV testing and serostatus. In 2013, the HCPI supported 18 community-based organizations (CBOs) across eight provinces, serving over 14,000 clients. Additionally, 6,000 clients accessed services at 103 HCPI-supported government health centers and four hospitals. While the Ministry of Health (MoH) has assumed responsibility for NSP, it must still secure funding for the millions of needles and syringes required annually. The MoH also increasingly funds MMT, ensuring its availability at numerous government health facilities. In Kenya, the Muslim Education and Welfare Association (MEWA) provides HIV prevention and drug dependency treatment in Mombasa and Kilifi counties. Their program improves access to clean needles, syringes, treatment, care, and socioeconomic support while advocating for opioid substitution therapy and the human rights of key populations. A focus on reuniting female drug users with their families has proven effective in supporting care engagement and retention. MEWA also offers free meals, reproductive health services, and accommodations for clients on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and tuberculosis (TB) treatment. Entrepreneurship training, job placement opportunities, and referrals to government micro-financing programs are also available. MEWA builds trust with clients through consistent contact, strong referral systems, and community-based mobile services. They also provide temporary custodial care and comprehensive support for children of drug users, including health, nutrition, and education services. Family reunification has been achieved for half of MEWA’s clients, and outreach efforts have increased service coverage for female drug users from 36% to 84%. Despite these successes, challenges persist, including resistance from law enforcement to NSP due to misconceptions about promoting drug use and crime. MEWA addresses these issues through community dialogue, police training workshops, and outreach worker presence in high-risk areas, fostering collaboration between the community, law enforcement, and MEWA staff. In Lebanon, the SIDC has provided harm reduction services since 1996, including the establishment of the first drop-in center for people who inject drugs in the Middle East. Their services include HIV testing and counseling, needle and syringe programs, opioid substitution therapy, and psychosocial and legal support. Advocacy efforts aim to reduce stigma and promote drug law reform, encouraging treatment over incarceration. In Mexico, Espolea targets young people aged 15–29 with harm reduction education at events like music festivals and cultural gatherings. They provide practical information on drug risks and safer practices through workshops, social media, and printed materials. Espolea also addresses stigma through evidence-based publications and workshops with policymakers. In Pakistan, the Nai Zindagi Trust has delivered harm reduction services for 25 years, prioritizing outreach over facility-based approaches. They involve people who inject drugs (PWID) in program design and implementation, with 30–40% of outreach workers being former injectors. Their services include needle and syringe programs, HIV prevention, and a residential ART adherence program. Nai Zindagi also trains staff and collaborates with public health systems to avoid duplicating services. In Tanzania, Médecins du Monde (MdM) provides harm reduction services with a focus on women and critical enablers for service uptake. They offer needle and syringe programs, income-generating activities, and legal referrals. MdM also supports the establishment of harm reduction committees and shelters for women and children. In Ukraine, harm reduction programs have reached up to 23% of PWID, with innovative approaches like peer-driven interventions (PDI) extending services to underserved groups. Pharmacies have been involved as secondary outlets for prevention commodities, increasing program coverage by 10% in some areas. In Vietnam, a pilot project decentralized HIV testing and care to commune health stations, promoting earlier diagnosis and treatment. Community outreach and trust-building were critical to facilitating access to services, with significant improvements in median CD4 counts at ART initiation. In Afghanistan, the Afghan Family Guidance Association (AFGA) provides harm reduction services for female prisoners, including advocacy for gender-sensitive approaches and training peer educators. Coordination with government ministries has improved prison healthcare delivery and referral networks. In Albania, STOP AIDS implemented an incentives program to encourage safer behaviors among young PWID. While successful in improving service uptake, further research is needed to assess the sustainability of behavior changes. In Indonesia, methadone maintenance therapy (MMT) was piloted in Kerobokan Prison, Bali, in 2005. In Iran, harm reduction efforts focus on opioid substitution therapy, with over 4,000 treatment centers offering services under medical supervision. Advocacy has shifted policies from zero-tolerance to harm reduction, addressing the concentrated HIV epidemic among PWID. These programs demonstrate the importance of comprehensive harm reduction strategies, community engagement, and collaboration with stakeholders to address the needs of vulnerable populations effectively.
